title: The Trinity in the New Testament and the Goodness of the Son
english: … it has supplied the solution through another Scripture. The New Testament, however, no longer speaks as in a shadow and behind a veil, but clearly and in so many words, as these witnesses show.

Paul writes to the Romans, “Since God is one” (Romans 3:30), and to the Galatians and the Corinthians, “God is one” (Galatians 3:20). And again to the Corinthians, in the second letter: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:14). Here, because the Godhead is the same, he mentioned the Son first, then the Father, and then his Holy Spirit. And he spoke of the communion of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son: a communion in the one Godhead, glory and kingdom. For what other communion could there be in God?

To the Ephesians he writes: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all” (Ephesians 4:5-6). Then to the same readers: “For this reason I bend my knees to the God and Father, from whom every family in the heavens and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man, so that Christ may dwell in the hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:14-17). Here again, in the same way, because the hypostases are equal in honour, he mentioned the Spirit first after the Father, and then the Son.
And again to the Corinthians: “I urge you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God for me” (Romans 15:30).

And to the Hebrews: “For if the word spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? It began to be spoken through the Lord, and it was confirmed to us by those who heard him, while God bore witness with them by signs and wonders and various mighty works, and by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will” (Hebrews 2:2-4). By “the Lord”, then, the Son is made known; by “God”, the Father; and then also the Holy Spirit, free in his own will and almighty.

The Son too showed the one Godhead by saying, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, God” (Mark 10:18); and he showed the three hypostases, equal in honour and equal in power, by his teaching on baptism (Matthew 28:19). To the lawyer who questioned him to test him he did not say, “Do not call me good,” but, “Why do you call me good?” So he showed that he himself is good, equally with the Father; that his own goodness shines out from the Father’s goodness; and that he is good, begotten of the Good.

“For if,” he says, “you know me to be good, and are not tying the word to ‘teacher’ as in ‘Well done, good servant’ (Matthew 25:21), and ‘The good man brings out good from the good treasure of his heart’ (Luke 6:45), and ‘Samuel was good with God and with men’ (1 Samuel 2:26), and ‘Saul, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, was good, taller than all Israel from the shoulders upward’ (1 Samuel 9:1-2), and ‘Good is the living dog, above the lion that is dead’ (Ecclesiastes 9:4), then take nothing away from the primal Good. Acknowledge me as God: not other than the Father in Godhead, but in hypostasis.”

For the Godhead of the two is one; otherwise the first Good would no longer be found to be one. “For you have read somewhere,” he says, “that ‘it is good for you to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man’ (Psalm 118:8), and ‘to cling to God is good’ (Psalm 73:28); and I have always urged you to follow me as good and to walk behind me.” That is why he did not say, “No one is good but one, the Father,” but, “No one is good but one, God,” just as he says somewhere else, “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do my words?” (Luke 6:46).

For creation, he says, has its goodness by participation. It imitates as far as it can, if one may say so, the innate and perfect goodness of God, and is preserved by it. The very existence of the good in creation is its sharing in God’s goodness, as it clings to him by obedience and by love for him. For it is written, “Those who remove themselves far from you will perish” (Psalm 73:27), and, “God is far from the ungodly” (Proverbs 15:29), and, “Salvation is far from sinners” (Psalm 119:155). Plainly this distance is one of relation and disposition, caused by opposition to the good and slowness toward virtue, and not one of place.

That he too is good, since by nature he is one with the good Father, he himself says in Matthew: “Or is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15); and again: “Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). And he said “the good portion” …

title: How Scripture Names the Three, Together and Apart
english: … himself. And they join in proclaiming it, by the Spirit: men unseen, yet men who kept very close company with the divine Spirit. Among the others who go along with them are these. The sacred psalmist, in Psalm 118: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Psalm 118:1); and in the same psalm: “Let all who fear the Lord now say that he is good” (Psalm 118:4). Jeremiah in his lament: “The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul that seeks him” (Lamentations 3:25). And Isaiah: “The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel” (Isaiah 63:7).

That the Holy Spirit of God is also good, David, whom I have mentioned, sings in a psalm: “Your good Spirit will lead me in a level land” (Psalm 143:10). Further: if eternal life is good, and the words of the Son are good (for he said, “I am the life” (John 14:6), and again, “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life” (John 6:63)); and if “the sanctification of the Holy Spirit” is good, and his working in illumination (for he is named with them as a fellow worker), and also the distribution of the heavenly gifts; then the Son and the Holy Spirit are certainly good.

We were not taught by hearing alone. We have also seen, as far as that is possible, what is proper to each hypostasis of the august and consubstantial Trinity: the Father saying from heaven, “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17); his Only-begotten being baptized on earth; and his one and only Holy Spirit coming down in the form of a dove and remaining upon the Only-begotten God and Son himself (John 1:32). A treasure of David in Psalm 85 confirms this too: that he who took flesh from our earthly nature was attested by God the Father as Son. The saying is known to all; it runs: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Psalm 85:11).

In the same way, because there is no difference of Godhead in the awesome and spotless Trinity, the oracles sometimes show the Father with the Son. So David says, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Psalm 110:1), and Paul, “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7). Sometimes they join the Father with the Holy Spirit, as when Haggai prophesies, “For I am with you, says the Lord Almighty, and my Spirit stands in your midst” (Haggai 2:4-5); and again, “Not by great power nor by strength, but by my Spirit, said the Lord Almighty” (Zechariah 4:6).

We must linger over this text. For since the heterodox sometimes say, when the Spirit is mentioned with the Father, that some power without a hypostasis of its own is meant, the text before us stands guarded against them. Isaiah too: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16). And again: “There the deer met and showed one another their faces. They passed by in number, and not one of them perished; one did not seek the other, because the Lord commanded them, and his Spirit gathered them together” (Isaiah 34:15-16). And Paul to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16); and again, “The love of God has been poured out in your hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5); and again, “But to us God has revealed it through his Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

At other times they name the Son alone, as when Isaiah prophesies, “And now, Lord, you are our Father; and we are clay, all of us the work of your hands” (Isaiah 64:8); and Paul to the Galatians: “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

At other times they proclaim the Only-begotten together with the Holy Spirit. So Paul writes to the Corinthians, “But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11); and to the Romans, “I speak the truth in Christ, I am not lying, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 9:1); and again, “For if the one who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive” (2 Corinthians 11:4).

And at other times Scripture mentions the Holy Spirit alone, as when Isaiah prophesies, “They disobeyed and provoked the Holy Spirit” (Isaiah 63:10), and again, “A Spirit came down from the Lord and guided them” (Isaiah 63:14); and Paul writes to the Corinthians, “But the fleshly man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:14). So too Stephen says in the Acts, “You resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51); and again, “We are witnesses of these words, and so is the Holy Spirit” (Acts 5:32), just as we commonly say, “Only we are here, and God.”

title: Scripture Names the Three in Any Order
english: And in John the Saviour too mentions the divine Spirit alone, saying, “But when he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you into all the truth” (John 16:13). The Acts likewise confirm this: “While Peter was pondering the word, the Holy Spirit said to him, ‘Rise, go down, and go with them without any hesitation, for I have sent them’” (Acts 10:19-20). And again: “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2). And again the Holy Spirit said to Peter, “Rise and go,” to the house of Cornelius.

And once more the apostolic Acts, with a certain elegance, give room to dwell on a statement of this kind. They contain: “Then Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to him” (Acts 13:9-10), and further: “For Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to the people” (Acts 4:8).

In the same way, the equal weight and equal power of the all-honoured hypostases is signified in this too: that the Master, God the Word, by his all-praised saying about baptism, which I mentioned before (Matthew 28:19), kept for himself and for the Holy Spirit their equality of honour with the Father. Because of it the sacred books sometimes mention the Father first and then the Son or the Holy Spirit, and sometimes mention the Son first, since the nature is undivided and there is no difference in the way the three are spoken of as God.

So Job, plainly showing the Trinity, says: “As the Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter: truly, while my breath is still in me, and the divine Spirit that remains to me in my nostrils” (Job 27:2-3). He means the Holy Spirit, who gives him life and still makes him breathe.

So too when Paul writes to the Thessalonians the second time: “Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God and Father, will comfort your hearts” (2 Thessalonians 2:16-17); and to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle, not from man nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Galatians 1:1); and to the Corinthians, as was said before: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and Father and the communion of the Holy Spirit” (2 Corinthians 13:14). And the Saviour says, “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Sometimes they name the Holy Spirit first, and afterwards the Father or the Son, as when David sings, “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and from your face where shall I flee?” (Psalm 139:7). And Job, showing his grateful mind, says, “It is the divine Spirit that made me, and the breath of the Almighty that teaches me” (Job 33:4). And so Paul writes in the first letter to the Corinthians: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4-6).

Sometimes they speak of two hypostases by the same name, as when Zechariah says, “The Lord said to the devil, ‘The Lord will rebuke you, devil’” (Zechariah 3:2). This was also shown above at greater length.
That what is said at one time of the Father is said at another of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, because the Trinity exists in one Godhead.

The revealers of holy things, then, knowing the glorious Trinity in one Godhead, and that what is said of it as God is shared in common, set forth at other times, some of them, about the Son or the Holy Spirit what others have just said about the Father. They do not contradict themselves. They do it so that we too may know this very point, the crucial thing in right faith: that whichever hypostasis we mention, we have by all means taken up the other with it in faith, since it cannot be separated.

The truthful interpreters of God must speak truly; and those who teach the simple and real truth of God, that is, his goodness, must be clean of every opinion that denies the truth. For they say it is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure; and these men were pure, and strangers to all false belief.

We shall find this at once in the vision of God that Isaiah saw. But why should I not first recall that whole passage as it stands? He says, then (Isaiah 6:1-3): “I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a throne high and lifted up, and the house was full of his glory. And seraphim stood around him; six wings to the one and six wings to the other; with two wings they covered their faces, with two their feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to the other, ‘Holy, holy …
